questions.prompt: Before my first day at the new job, I felt completely ___ by the size of the company.
questions.note: Daunted = feeling that something is too big or too difficult for you. The -ed form describes how a person feels; the -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling: The company was daunting. I was daunted.
why: Daunting describes the thing, not the person: a daunting task. I felt daunting would mean that you frightened other people. It works exactly like boring and bored.
Daunt is the base verb (Nothing daunts her). After felt you need an adjective, so use the participle daunted.
Dauntingly is an adverb: it describes an adjective (a dauntingly long list). After felt you need an adjective, not an adverb.

questions.prompt: Out of the blue, the bank returned €400 in old fees. What a lovely ___!
questions.note: Windfall = money you get suddenly and did not expect. The word first meant fruit blown down by the wind — free to pick up. Common partners: a tax windfall, an unexpected windfall, windfall profits.
why: Rainfall is the amount of rain that falls in a place. It also ends in -fall, but it is a weather word, not a money word.
Payday is the day you receive your salary — money you expect and work for. Here the money came out of the blue.
A bargain is something you buy for less than its usual price. Here nobody bought anything; the money simply arrived.

questions.prompt: Ana scored three goals in one match — her first ___ of the season.
questions.note: A hat trick is three goals by one player in one game, or more generally three successes in a row. It comes from cricket, where a bowler who did this could win a new hat.
why: A home run comes from baseball and means one big, clear success. It is a single hit, not three goals, and it sounds very American.
A three-pointer is a single basketball shot worth three points. It is one shot in a different sport, not three goals.
A top hat is a tall, formal hat. It contains the word hat, but it is just clothing, not a sports idiom.

questions.prompt: We stayed in a small ___ hotel — the owners lived on the top floor and cooked breakfast themselves.
questions.note: Noun + past participle makes a compact adjective: family-owned = owned by a family. Keep the hyphen before a noun: battery-powered, home-cooked, snow-covered.
why: The first part never takes -s, even when the meaning is plural: a family-owned shop, not families-owned.
The order is fixed: noun first, then the participle. Owned-family is not a word, and it sounds like a family that someone owns.
The -ing form gives an active meaning: a family-owning hotel would be a hotel that owns a family. The hotel is owned, so use the past participle owned.

questions.prompt: The meeting was moved from Friday to Monday morning, so everyone ___ to finish their slides over the weekend.
questions.note: Scramble to do something = hurry to do something in a rush, usually because time is short.
why: Squabble means to argue about something small (squabble over the front seat). It takes over/about, not to + verb, and nobody is arguing here.
Scribble means to write quickly and carelessly (scribble a note). It needs an object and is about handwriting, not about hurrying to finish work.
Stumble means to almost fall while walking, or to make mistakes when speaking (stumble over a word). It does not mean hurrying.

questions.prompt: A burst pipe ___ havoc in the basement while we were away.
questions.note: Wreak havoc /riːk ˈhævək/ = cause a lot of damage and confusion. Wreak is an old verb that rhymes with week; today it lives mainly in this phrase.
why: A very common mistake, even among native speakers. Wreck does mean “destroy”, but you wreck a thing (wreck the car); the fixed phrase is wreak havoc.
Cause havoc is correct English, but havoc is uncountable and takes no article: not a havoc, just havoc.
Break does not combine with havoc. You can break a pipe, but you wreak or cause havoc.

questions.prompt: ___ late for the interview, he also forgot his CV.
questions.note: When a sentence opens with not only, the helping verb moves in front of the subject, just as in a question. With be, the verb be itself moves: Not only was he late…
why: This is statement word order. After not only at the start, invert: Not only was he… Normal order is fine only when not only sits inside the sentence: He was not only late…
Be never needs do to invert: it moves to the front on its own, as in Was he late?, not Did he be late?
The inversion is right, but the verb must agree with the subject: he was, so was he. Were he appears only in formal conditionals (Were he here, …).

options: He can boil an egg, let alone cook dinner.
He can’t boil an egg, let alone cooking dinner.
He can’t cook dinner, let alone boil an egg.
He can’t boil an egg, let alone cook dinner.
questions.note: Let alone = and certainly not. Three things must be right: the first part is negative, the idea after let alone is bigger and even less likely, and both parts match in form (verb after verb: boil … cook).
why: The first part must be negative. He can boil an egg is positive, so let alone has nothing to build on.
Both parts must match: boil is a base verb, so the second part needs one too — cook, not cooking.
The order is reversed. The smaller, easier thing comes first and the bigger one after let alone. Cooking dinner is harder than boiling an egg, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Most buyers loved the flat but ___ the price and walked away.
questions.note: Balk at something /bɔːk/ = refuse because it feels too expensive, too risky or too much. It rhymes with talk and walk: the l is silent. The spelling baulk appears in older British texts.
why: Jump at means to accept something eagerly (jump at the chance) — the opposite. Buyers who jumped at the price would not walk away.
Stick at means to keep working hard at something difficult (stick at your English). It does not describe refusing a price.
Right verb, wrong preposition. Balk combines with at: balk at the cost, balk at the idea, balk at paying.

questions.prompt: The report warns of a ___ of qualified nurses in rural hospitals.
questions.note: A dearth of something /dɜːθ/ = too little of it; very few. It rhymes with earth and belongs to reports, articles and formal speech. With friends, say not enough or a shortage of.
why: Death /deθ/ looks almost the same, but it means the end of life. The two words differ by one letter and one vowel sound.
A wealth of means a lot of something (a wealth of experience) — the opposite. A report would not warn about having plenty of nurses.
Shortness describes being short in length or time (shortness of breath). For too few of something, use a shortage of or a dearth of.

questions.prompt: ___ that the airport cancelled every morning flight.
options: So thick did the fog be
questions.note: In literary English, so + adjective can move to the front for effect. Then the verb comes before the subject: So thick was the fog that… Keep the that clause — it carries the result. In everyday speech, say The fog was so thick that…
why: With so + adjective at the front, the subject and verb must swap: was the fog, not the fog was.
Such goes with a noun (such thick fog that…), not with an adjective on its own. Before a bare adjective, use so.
Be inverts on its own and never takes do: was the fog, not did the fog be.

questions.prompt: When the mayor ___ the project, the money appeared within a week.
questions.note: Throw your weight behind something = support it with all your power and influence. The weight belongs to the subject: she threw her weight behind it, they threw their weight behind it.
why: Throw your weight around is a real idiom, but it means using your power in a bossy, unpleasant way. It takes no object, so it cannot be followed by the project.
The idiom needs a possessive that matches the subject: her weight. The weight breaks the fixed phrase.
Pull your weight means to do your fair share of work in a team (Everyone must pull their weight). It does not combine with behind.
